_doc.purpose: There is no such thing as an unobtainable material. There are materials that are SOMEWHERE ELSE, and the question is only what it costs to go and get them. This file says where each thing is, how hard the place is to reach, and what you need in order to reach it. It replaces the 'tier 9 unobtainable' concept entirely.
three_ways_to_get_a_distant_material: TRADE: pay a chain of middlemen. Cheapest to start, most expensive per unit, and you never control supply.
EXPEDITION and FACTORY: send your own ships, establish a trading post. Large capital, large risk, controls supply.
CONQUEST or COLONY: take the source. Largest capital, largest risk, largest moral cost, and it is what actually happened historically for rubber, saltpetre, spices and silver.
_doc.note_on_ubiquity: Materials with ubiquity 'everywhere' are not modelled as located: wood, clay, sand, stone, water, common earths. They only matter if a SPECIFIC variety is local, which is flagged per material.
_doc.note_on_reach_from_italia_and_geometry: THIS FILE USED TO BE ROME-CENTRIC AND THAT WAS A BUG. Every region carried one hard-coded 'reach' number measured from Italy, and the simulator's `civs` command printed it and did nothing else: `reach` was never read anywhere that computed a cost. Play Han China and the model still treated Chinese silk as 'reach 3, far away' and Malaya, which Chinese and Malay traders already sail to routinely, as an exotic reach-3 frontier, while it treated ITALY as reach 0 for a civilization that has never seen Italy. That is backwards for any civilization but Rome. The fix: every region now carries a `lat`/`lon` centroid, a `coastal` flag and a `route_difficulty` multiplier, so sim/simulator.py can compute a great-circle distance from ANY civilization's own home centroid and derive a reach band for THAT civilization, modified by how far it already routinely travels (`base_reach` in the civilization file) and by whether the destination is reachable by sea. The old per-region `reach` field is kept, renamed to `reach_from_italia`, purely as the historical Roman special case: it is what a Roman-centric build of this file used to call 'reach', it is no longer read as if it applied to every civilization, and it also serves as the calibration anchor for material cost multipliers below (see `located_materials._note`).
_doc.note_on_land: Added for Complaints/43's second half: iugerum_land solving to 0.0 because nothing modelled WHERE arable land is or how good it is. Each region's own `land` block gives land_area_km2 (the region's real, coarse land area), arable_fraction (the share of that area physically capable of supporting pre-industrial rain-fed or simple-irrigation farming - a terrain/climate fact, not a farmed-today fact) and fertility_quality_multiplier (a yield multiplier on the arable share, 1.0 being data/production/40_organics.json's own Roman-Italian wheat_kg baseline - the SAME convention sim/world/agriculture.py's Land(hectares, quality=...) already uses, chosen deliberately so a later integration between the two needs no rename). Both are COUNTRY-SCALE APPROXIMATIONS from general geography (land area of the modern states each region coarsely groups; arable share and fertility from well-known climate/terrain/soil facts about those same places), not a surveyed GIS/soil dataset this project does not have - see each region's own `land.source` and sim/world/land.py's own module docstring for what a more precise version would need. A civilisation's own cultivable land is the SUM of this over the regions named in its `home_regions` (data/civilizations/*.json), never a constant - see sim/world/land.py.

regions._note: lat/lon are coarse centroids in degrees (negative = south / west), good enough for great-circle banding, not for navigation. coastal marks whether the region is reachable and workable by sea rather than only overland; a landlocked region can still be reached, just more slowly and without the sea-going discount a coastal society gets. route_difficulty multiplies the raw great-circle distance to approximate a real voyage's difficulty where straight-line distance badly understates it (ice, blue-water crossings with no coastal stepping-stones, hostile mountain and desert relay routes) or slightly overstates it (a fast, reliable, wind-assisted route like the monsoon crossing to India). minerals gives each region's rough share of a material's total output AT THIS TECHNOLOGICAL LEVEL, normalised so Rome's own home regions sum to about 1.0 per metal -- this reproduces data/world/resources.json's Roman totals for a Roman-home-region civilization exactly, and gives every other civilization the same yardstick for ITS OWN ground instead of the population-scaled guess the simulator used to make.

italia.name: Italy
italia.note: Home, if you are Rome. Nobody else's home.

land.source: Land area is modern Italy's. arable_fraction (~23%) is the commonly-cited modern national arable-land share, taken as a proxy for the terrain/climate constraint (Apennine spine versus the Po valley and coastal plains) rather than for anything about who farms it today. fertility_quality_multiplier is DEFINITIONAL, not estimated: data/production/40_organics.json's own wheat_kg entry (577.5 kg/ha net) IS Roman/Italian dry-farmed wheat, so Italia is the 1.0 reference point sim/world/agriculture.py's own Land(hectares, quality=1.0) already uses 'ordinary Mediterranean loam' for - every other region's multiplier is stated relative to this one.

gaul_germania.name: Gaul and the Germanies
gaul_germania.note: Noricum steel is famous; this is also the Rhineland and Ruhr coal country long before anyone calls it that, which is why it matters so much to whoever holds it in 1300.

land.source: Land area sums modern France, Germany and the Low Countries, this region's rough modern equivalents. arable_fraction ~30% reflects temperate lowland (Paris Basin, north German plain) against the Alps, Massif Central and Black Forest. fertility below Italia's 1.0: real loess and river-valley soils here are good, but a cooler, wetter, shorter growing season than the Mediterranean holds ancient dry-farmed grain yield somewhat below it - direction well attested, size a placeholder.

britannia.name: Britain
britannia.note: Cornish tin, Mendip and Pennine lead, Wealden iron, and coalfields the Romans barely touch. THIS is where the coal actually is; a civilization that HOLDS Britain should not be treated as coal-poor just because it has few people.

land.source: Land area is Great Britain's. arable_fraction ~25% (much of Scotland and Wales is upland moor, per this region's own note about it being pastoral country too). fertility below temperate-Continental gaul_germania: a cooler, cloudier maritime climate than even northern Gaul, well attested qualitatively; the multiplier's size is not.

hispania.name: Iberia
hispania.note: Rio Tinto and Cartagena. The single richest metal ground in the Roman world and the reason the denarius exists.

land.source: Land area sums modern Spain and Portugal. arable_fraction ~25% (fertile Guadalquivir/Ebro valleys and coastal plains against the arid Meseta interior). fertility close to Italia's: genuinely Mediterranean climate, slightly below on account of the drier interior plateau this one region-wide average has to include.

Land area sums modern Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt - overwhelmingly Sahara desert, which is why arable_fraction is only ~4% even though it sums each country's own (very unequal) modern arable share (Morocco and Tunisia's Mediterranean coastal strips are in the high teens per cent; Egypt and Libya are a few per cent, almost entirely the Nile ribbon). fertility is high, not low, because this field prices ONLY the arable sliver, and that sliver is dominated by Nile silt - among the most fertile soil on Earth, the reason Egypt was Rome's breadbasket. 1.35 sits just under sim/world/agriculture.py's own NILE_FLOOD_RECESSION_SOIL_FERTILITY_YIELD_MULTIPLIER (1.4, independently re-derived here rather than imported - see this module's own STANDALONE note), pulled down slightly by the Maghreb coastal share, which is good land but not Nile-grade.

greece_anatolia.name: Greece and Anatolia
greece_anatolia.note: Laurion silver funded the Athenian navy long before Rome got here.

land.source: Land area sums modern Greece and Turkey. arable_fraction ~28% (Anatolian plateau against genuinely mountainous, thin-soiled Greece). fertility below Italia's: Mediterranean climate, but rockier terrain and thinner soils than the Po valley or Campania - Greek grain dependence on imported (including Egyptian and Black Sea) wheat is the historical symptom of exactly this.

levant_mesopotamia.name: Syria and Mesopotamia
levant_mesopotamia.note: Cyprus copper (the metal is named after the island) sits at this end of the Mediterranean.

land.source: Land area sums modern Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel/Palestine. arable_fraction ~20% (river valleys and the Levantine coast against the Syrian and Jordanian desert). fertility is high: the Tigris-Euphrates floodplain is the literal Fertile Crescent, agriculture's own place of origin, and irrigated Mesopotamian yields were historically excellent - below north_africa's Nile figure because Nile silt is replenished by an annual flood essentially free of labour, where Mesopotamian irrigation needs continuous canal maintenance to keep delivering it.

scandinavia.name: Scandinavia and the Baltic
scandinavia.note: Outside the Empire but reachable by trade. Amber road is ancient. Bog iron, smelted from ore raked out of lakebeds, is real and is what the Norse actually work with (met_bloomery_bog_iron); it is decent for tools and blades and no substitute for a coalfield.

land.source: Land area sums Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Finland. arable_fraction ~8% (Denmark alone is flat and largely farmable, but it is small; Norway and much of Sweden/Finland are forest, mountain or lake). fertility below Britannia's: a shorter, cooler growing season and more podzolic soils, but this is boreal-temperate farmland actually worked for millennia (southern Sweden, Denmark), not the tundra sim/world/agriculture.py's own ARCTIC_TUNDRA (0.05) describes - the two must not be confused, which is why this number sits well above it.

arabia_horn.name: Arabia and the Horn of Africa

land.source: Land area sums the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa. arable_fraction ~2% (the Peninsula is almost entirely desert but for a few oases and Yemen's terraced highlands; the Horn's Ethiopian highlands are the real exception). fertility 0.50 blends genuinely decent highland farmland (Ethiopia's volcanic highland soil and reliable highland rainfall historically supported dense population) with marginal desert-margin and oasis farming elsewhere in the region, which is most of its small arable share by area.

india.name: India and Ceylon
india.note: ALREADY REACHABLE IN 100 AD by the monsoon route, Berenice to Muziris. Rome runs this trade annually and Pliny complains about the bullion drain. route_difficulty is BELOW 1 here on purpose: the monsoon is a scheduled, reliable wind system, not an obstacle, and treating it as ordinary distance understates how easy this crossing actually is once you know the timing. Also the world's dominant saltpetre source (Bengal), see located_materials.

land.source: Land area sums the Indian subcontinent and Ceylon. arable_fraction ~50% is unusually high among large regions in this file - the Indo-Gangetic plain is one of the largest contiguous alluvial lowlands on Earth, and modern India is repeatedly cited as having one of the highest arable-land shares of any large country, a terrain fact rather than a modern-farming one. fertility is high: Gangetic alluvium plus a monsoon that (unlike Mediterranean dry farming) supports rice, which yields more calories per hectare than wheat under comparable technology - below the Nile's annual-flood figure because monsoon rainfall is a less reliable input than an annual silt flood.

persia_centralasia.name: Persia and Central Asia
persia_centralasia.note: Silk Road via Palmyra. Parthia is hostile but trade passes. Not coastal in this model: the Persian Gulf littoral exists but the bulk of the region, and the route through it, is overland relay across mountains and desert, which is why route_difficulty is above 1.

land.source: Land area sums Iran, Afghanistan and the Central Asian states this region's own note describes as reached by Silk Road relay. arable_fraction ~10% (river-valley oases - the Oxus and Jaxartes basins above all - against the Iranian plateau's aridity and Afghanistan's mountains). fertility 0.55: oasis irrigation is genuinely productive where it exists, well above true desert, but this is still a water-constrained region overall, not a soil-rich one.

china.name: China
china.note: Reachable by Silk Road relay and by sea via India. Roman embassy recorded at the Han court in 166 AD. Shanxi coal and iron are enormous by any pre-modern standard, which is exactly why Han China starts this simulator already holding the blast furnace and cast iron: the ground supports it.

land.source: Land area is modern China's. arable_fraction ~13% (the Tibetan plateau, the Gobi and Xinjiang's deserts, and the western mountains dominate China's total area; the arable share is concentrated in the North China Plain, the Loess Plateau and the Yangtze basin). fertility is high, matching this file's own note that 'Shanxi coal and iron are enormous... which is exactly why Han China starts this simulator already holding the blast furnace': Yellow River loess and Yangtze rice-paddy country are both historically exceptional farmland, comparable to the Nile or the Fertile Crescent.

west_africa.name: West and Central Africa
west_africa.note: Coastal. Hanno the Carthaginian sailed down this coast c. 500 BC. Not hard, merely not done. West African iron-working (the Nok tradition and its successors) is real and older than most people assume; it is not a large exportable surplus by Roman-scale demand, hence the modest share.

land.source: Land area sums the major states of West and Central Africa this region groups (Nigeria, Ghana, Cote d'Ivoire, Senegal, Mali, Cameroon, DR Congo and neighbours). arable_fraction ~15% is a rough share cultivable outside dense rainforest interior and Sahel desert fringe. fertility below Italia's despite abundant rainfall: tropical rainforest soils are well documented in agronomy as heavily leached and nutrient-poor beneath a lush canopy, a genuine pedological fact, not a climate-severity one.

southeast_asia.name: Malaya, Indonesia, the Spice Islands
southeast_asia.note: Malayan tin is real and additional to the Cornwall/Iberia figures above, not a slice of them.

land.source: Land area sums Indonesia and Malaysia, this region's own 'Malaya, Indonesia, the Spice Islands' description. arable_fraction ~12% (dense equatorial rainforest limits cleared cropland at this era's technology). fertility above Italia's: volcanic soils on Java and Sumatra are repeatedly cited among the most fertile in the tropics, which is also why Java alone has historically supported extremely dense population.

east_africa_south.name: East Africa and the Cape
east_africa_south.note: Herodotus reports a Phoenician circumnavigation of Africa under Necho II. Contested, but the voyage is physically possible with era-appropriate ships; route_difficulty reflects a long, mostly unprecedented coastal haul, not an ocean crossing.

land.source: Land area sums South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Mozambique, Tanzania and Kenya - this region's own 'East Africa and the Cape' span. arable_fraction ~10% (savanna and semi-arid bushland, much of it historically tsetse-affected and poor for cultivation, dominate; the East African highlands and the Cape's own Mediterranean-climate corner are the exceptions). fertility 0.70: decent highland and highveld grassland soils, below the best alluvial regions but well above true desert or leached rainforest.

siberia_urals.name: The Urals and Siberia
siberia_urals.note: Overland-reachable through Scythian and Sarmatian trade (see platinum in located_materials). Genuinely mineral-rich ground; genuinely hard to get a wagon to.

land.source: Land area is a round figure for Siberia and the Urals. arable_fraction ~3% (permafrost and boreal taiga dominate; only the southern steppe fringe near the Urals and the West Siberian Plain is workable). fertility 0.50: the workable southern fringe includes real steppe soil related to the same chernozem belt sim/world/agriculture.py's own UKRAINIAN_CHERNOZEM describes further west, but a short growing season this far north and this file's own coarse regional average keep it well below that entry's 1.4.

americas_carib.name: The Caribbean and Mesoamerica
americas_carib.note: No draught animals and no iron-working tradition here, but the ore exists in the ground; copper and gold are what the Mexica actually work, which is why iron is a small share and copper a large one.

land.source: Land area sums Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean islands. arable_fraction ~14% (the Mexican highland valleys and Caribbean coastal plains against arid northern Mexico and tropical forest further south). fertility close to Italia's: the volcanic soils of the Valley of Mexico historically supported one of the densest pre-industrial populations anywhere via chinampa cultivation, offset by the region's large arid and tropical-forest shares elsewhere.

americas_south.name: South America, Amazonia and the Andes
americas_south.note: Andean silver (Potosi and its neighbours) is one of the largest silver endowments on Earth; the share here is deliberately generous rather than conservative.

land.source: Land area is the South American continent's. arable_fraction is low (~6%) because Amazonia - most of the continent's area - is rainforest whose soil, like West Africa's, is thin and heavily leached beneath the canopy, a well-documented ecological fact; the true farmland is concentrated in the Andean terraces and the Pampas. fertility reflects that smaller arable share rather than Amazonia's much larger area: Andean terracing is workmanlike but not exceptional, the Pampas grassland is excellent (comparable to a prairie Mollisol), and the blend lands close to Italia's baseline.

Land area sums the United States and Canada. arable_fraction ~12% (the Great Plains and eastern woodlands against the Canadian Shield's boreal forest and the northern tundra fringe). fertility above Italia's: North American prairie soils (Mollisols) are geologically comparable to the Ukrainian chernozem sim/world/agriculture.py's own table already treats as exceptional (1.4) - held below that figure here because this region's average also has to include its large boreal and eastern-woodland shares, which are ordinary rather than exceptional.

Land area is Australia's (Pacific islands add negligibly to it). arable_fraction is small (~6%) because the interior is arid to semi-arid desert; the workable land is a coastal fringe, mostly in the southeast and southwest. fertility, for that fringe, is below Italia's: Australian soils are geologically among the oldest and most weathered, and therefore most mineral-depleted, in the world, a well documented pedological fact distinct from the aridity arable_fraction already charges for.

greenland_arctic.name: Greenland and the Arctic
greenland_arctic.note: route_difficulty is the highest in the file on purpose: raw distance from most of Eurasia is not actually that large (Greenland is closer to Rome in a straight line than India is), but the ice-bound approach is what makes it hard, and only ships built for exactly this (Norse clinker hulls, base_reach 4) shrug it off. Distance alone would badly under-price this region.

land.source: Land area is Greenland's. arable_fraction is close to zero (~80% ice-capped; the ice-free fringe is tundra, of which only a handful of low-Arctic fjord meadows in the far south were ever used at all, historically for hay and grazing rather than grain). fertility matches sim/world/agriculture.py's own ARCTIC_TUNDRA quality multiplier (0.05) exactly, for the same reason that module gives: the limiting factor is growing-season length, not soil fertility, which this single scalar cannot separate from fertility any better here than it can there.

1.desc: close to home ground, inside the same cultural and trading sphere

2.desc: established trade routes exist and this civilization already uses them

3.desc: known to exist, no regular traffic yet, coastal sailing sufficient

4.desc: long open-water or deep-continental voyage, needs provisioning against scurvy and a real hull

5.desc: ocean crossing, needs open-ocean navigation and a ship that survives it

6.desc: the far ocean or the ice

located_materials._note: cost_multiplier is what a kilogramme costs delivered to Italy relative to producing it locally, by TRADE, at the start, FOR ROME SPECIFICALLY (that is the civilization this number was originally written for, and reach_from_italia above is its calibration point). sim/simulator.py's Sim.material_reach() turns this into a cost multiplier for WHATEVER civilization you are actually playing, by comparing that civilization's own geometric reach to the region against reach_from_italia: at civ_reach 0 (you live there) the multiplier is 1, at civ_reach == reach_from_italia it reproduces this number exactly (which is why Rome's own numbers barely move), and at civ_reach below reach_from_italia -- the whole point of this fix -- it comes out CHEAPER, because the material genuinely is closer for that civilization. An expedition or a colony then cuts it further, which is the whole economic argument for both.

rubber_latex.note: THE CLASSIC 'UNOBTAINABLE' AND IT IS NOT. Hevea brasiliensis is Amazonian, but Landolphia and Funtumia vines in West and Central Africa also yield real rubber and were the basis of a huge industry in the 1890s. West Africa is coastal sailing from the Pillars of Hercules, which Hanno did around 500 BC. You do not need to cross an ocean for rubber. You need to sail down a coast and know which vine to tap.

gutta_percha.note: Palaquium latex, Malaya. Reachable by extending the existing India route east, which Indian and Malay traders already do. Traders based IN China or India are already doing most of this journey as a matter of routine; the old Rome-only reach model could not say that.

cinchona_bark.note: Andean, and genuinely only Andean until the 19th-century transplants to Java and India. Malaria is endemic around Rome, so this is worth an ocean crossing on its own. Once you have it, transplant it: the Dutch and British both did.

sodium_nitrate.note: Atacama caliche. Enormous, but you do not need it: Indian saltpetre from Bengal was the world's supply for centuries and is reachable on a route Rome already sails, and nitre beds work anywhere.

potassium_nitrate_natural.note: BENGAL SALTPETRE. This is the important one and almost every bootstrap plan misses it. Natural nitre efflorescence on the Gangetic plain supplied the world's gunpowder for centuries. It is on a route Rome already sails annually. You can buy saltpetre instead of farming it, which removes the 24-month nitre-bed delay from the critical path entirely.

cryolite.note: Ivigtut, Greenland, essentially the only workable deposit. But synthetic fluoride baths from your own hydrofluoric acid work, which is what industry moved to anyway. Genuinely close to home for the Norse (base_reach 4, ships built for ice-bound coasts) and genuinely remote for everyone else, which is exactly the asymmetry this file exists to capture.

platinum.note: Colombian placers and Ural placers. The Urals are overland-reachable through Scythian and Sarmatian trade.

potato.note: A crop, not a commodity. You need SEED STOCK once, then you grow it. One successful voyage changes the caloric ceiling of European agriculture permanently. Potatoes yield 2 to 4 times the calories per hectare of wheat on poor ground.

silk_raw.note: Rome already buys it. The sericulture SECRET is the valuable thing; two monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Byzantium in 552 AD, so it is stealable.

cloves_nutmeg.note: Maluku only, until transplanted. The single highest value-per-weight cargo in the pre-modern world.

pepper.note: Rome buys this by the shipload already.

wootz_ingot.note: Crucible steel ingots. Rome imports these. Buying the product is not the same as knowing the process, but it lets you reverse-engineer it.

amber.note: Also the best natural electrical insulator available to you, and the origin of the word electricity.

mercury.note: Almaden, an imperial monopoly, so this is a political cost not a distance cost.

bitumen_naphtha.note: Surface seeps. Your entire petroleum industry starts here and needs no drilling.

boric_acid.note: Larderello fumaroles, Tuscany. Verify on arrival.

argyrodite_germanium.note: Freiberg, Saxony, outside the Empire in free Germania. Zinc smelter flue dust is the better route anyway.

guano.note: Peruvian islands. Enormous nitrogen and phosphate resource, and it is why the guano trade mattered so much in the 19th century.

ivory_gold_west_africa.note: The West African gold trade is why the trans-Saharan routes existed. Reachable by sea, which is exactly what the Portuguese did to cut out the Saharan middlemen.
